explanation: Computer systems employ a memory hierarchy to balance speed and cost.  Faster, smaller memories (caches) are placed closer to the CPU, while slower, larger memories (main memory) are further away. Caching strategies leverage locality of reference (temporal and spatial) to improve performance by storing frequently accessed data in faster caches.  This reduces average memory access time.
syntax:
Cache organization is typically described using parameters: 
* C: Cache size (bytes)
* B: Block size (bytes)
* S: Number of sets
* E: Number of lines per set (associativity)
* b: Block offset bits (log₂B)
* s: Set index bits (log₂S)
* t: Tag bits (32 or 64 - b - s)
code_example:
; Example parameters for a direct-mapped cache (E=1)
; C = 1KB, B = 4 bytes
; Calculate S, s, b, t assuming a 32-bit address
; B = 4 bytes => b = log₂(4) = 2 bits
; C = 1KB = 1024 bytes => S = C/B = 256 sets
; s = log₂(S) = log₂(256) = 8 bits
; t = 32 - b - s = 32 - 2 - 8 = 22 bits
; Address format: |22 bits tag|8 bits set index|2 bits block offset|
example_explanation: This example demonstrates how to calculate the parameters of a direct-mapped cache given its size and block size.  A direct-mapped cache has only one line per set (E=1), meaning each memory block maps to a unique cache location determined by the set index bits. The tag bits identify the specific memory block within that set. The block offset indicates the location of a word within the block.  This design simplifies cache access but might suffer from conflict misses if multiple frequently accessed blocks map to the same set.

extraction_metadata.source: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (3rd Edition)
